title: OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan set to be freed on $1 million bond
excerpt: Judge Alex Tse allows Saudi ex-OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan to await trial at home. Alfozan will post $500,000 toward a $1 million bond.
content_html:
The Saudi engineer accused of bugging OpenAI is set to be released on a $1 million bond

By Stephen Council

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

2026-11-24T20:15:38.070Z

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the former OpenAI engineer who was fired and arrested in October on allegations that he bugged the company's office, is set to be released on a $1 million bond.

He'll be freed when his $500,000 share of that bond is posted, likely Wednesday — so he's set to be home in Millbrae, California, for Thanksgiving. He'll be fitted with an ankle monitor.

The decision, made by Magistrate Judge Alex Tse in a Tuesday hearing, marks a surprising reversal in the high-profile case. Tse had previously ordered that Alfozan remain in detention over concerns that he might flee to his home country of Saudi Arabia.

Alfozan then switched lawyers to defense attorney David Rizk, who pushed to get the engineer released from custody. Rizk excoriated the prosecution for surfacing discovery evidence too slowly and said they hadn't revealed anything indicating that Alfozan was a "spy" who'd committed economic espionage.

The former OpenAI employee is charged with using a device to intercept oral communications. He pleaded not guilty.

Rizk said after the hearing on Tuesday that he's "glad the court made the right decision," and told Business Insider that if all goes smoothly with Alfozan's release, he plans to delay the trial. The trial is scheduled for January.

Alfozan still has shares in OpenAI, fed says

During the Tuesday hearing, Assistant US Attorney Nick Parker, the case's lead prosecutor, said that Alfozan should remain detained.

He said the engineer remains a flight risk, stressing that Alfozan has fewer ties to the area since his wife and child have flown to Saudi Arabia and that he now has no job.

Parker also said that Alfozan has stock options from his time at OpenAI that have already vested, and so can't be "clawed back."

Judge Tse asked, "Even if he's convicted?"

Parker said that Alfozan could owe restitution if he's convicted, but his understanding is that when OpenAI goes public in its initial public offering — expected next year — the former employee will be able to cash out some shares.

Alfozan started at OpenAI in 2025. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Alfozan will turn in $500,000 and have his movements restricted

Judge Tse is getting Alfozan released on several conditions.

First, Alfozan gave Rizk a power of attorney so he could initiate the process of transferring $500,000 from a Robinhood account to a bank account and then to the court. He won't be released until that money is posted; Rizk said he's hoping to send it on Wednesday.

Alfozan will then need to report to pretrial officials to be fitted with an ankle monitor. He's barred from leaving his residence between 7 p.m. and 7 a.m., and is ordered to avoid airports, train depots, and other major transit centers. The government has already taken his travel documents. He isn't supposed to leave California's Northern District, which stretches along the coast from the Bay Area.

He also isn't allowed to access OpenAI records or information except through the case's discovery process.

If he reneges on any of these conditions, the government can come for the bond money. Alongside Alfozan's $500,000, three of his friends committed Tuesday to covering the remaining bond amount if need be.
